title: What are the array declaration and initialization forms (`int[] a = new int[5]`, `int[] a = {1,2,3}`, `int a[]`), what is the default value for each element type (0/false/null), and why is `int[] a` preferred over `int a[]` by convention?
shortTitle: What are the array declaration and initialization forms in Java?

s1_definition.profdef: A Java array is a fixed-size, contiguous container of elements of a single type, and it is an object allocated on the heap with a final `length` field. You can declare and create one with `new`, as in `int[] a = new int[5]`, which allocates five slots initialized to the type's default, or with an array initializer, as in `int[] a = {1, 2, 3}`, which both creates and fills it. The brackets may legally appear after the variable name, as in `int a[]`, but convention places them after the type, as in `int[] a`, because the brackets are part of the type, not the variable. Each element receives a default value when the array is created: numeric types default to zero, boolean to false, char to the null character, and reference types to null.
s1_definition.analogy: Think of an array as a row of fixed, numbered pigeonholes in the bank's mailroom, decided once and never resized. When Rajesh asks for a row of five number slots, the bank hands him five slots already stamped with zero, because an empty number slot defaults to zero. If he asks for a row of object slots, each slot is empty, meaning null, until he puts something in. He can either ask for a blank row of a certain size and fill it later, or hand over the exact contents up front and let the bank build a row sized to match. Writing the row-shape marker next to the type rather than the label is the house style, because the shape describes what KIND of thing the row holds, not the name on the row.
s1_definition.oneliner: Arrays are fixed-size heap objects; create them with new or an initializer, elements default to zero, false, or null, and put the brackets on the type because the brackets are part of the type.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A Java array is a fixed-size, contiguous container of elements of a single type, and it is an object allocated on the heap with a final `length` field. You can declare and create one with `new`, as in `int[] a = new int[5]`, which allocates five slots initialized to the type's default, or with an array initializer, as in `int[] a = {1, 2, 3}`, which both creates and fills it. The brackets may legally appear after the variable name, as in `int a[]`, but convention places them after the type, as in `int[] a`, because the brackets are part of the type, not the variable. Each element receives a default value when the array is created: numeric types default to zero, boolean to false, char to the null character, and reference types to null.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Think of an array as a row of fixed, numbered pigeonholes in the bank's mailroom, decided once and never resized. When Rajesh asks for a row of five number slots, the bank hands him five slots already stamped with zero, because an empty number slot defaults to zero. If he asks for a row of object slots, each slot is empty, meaning null, until he puts something in. He can either ask for a blank row of a certain size and fill it later, or hand over the exact contents up front and let the bank build a row sized to match. Writing the row-shape marker next to the type rather than the label is the house style, because the shape describes what KIND of thing the row holds, not the name on the row.

**One line to remember:** Arrays are fixed-size heap objects; create them with new or an initializer, elements default to zero, false, or null, and put the brackets on the type because the brackets are part of the type.

sections.s2_technical:
There are several ways to declare and create an array. The explicit form separates declaration and allocation: `int[] balances; balances = new int[5];`. The combined form does both: `int[] balances = new int[5];`, which allocates five int slots. The array initializer form both creates and fills: `int[] seed = {100, 200, 300};`, where the size is inferred from the number of elements. There is also the anonymous array form used when passing directly to a method or reassigning later: `process(new int[]{100, 200, 300});`. The initializer shorthand with braces can only be used at the point of declaration; you cannot write `int[] a; a = {1, 2, 3};` because the bare brace form is only legal in a declaration, so you would use `a = new int[]{1, 2, 3};` instead.

Every array has a public final `length` field, not a method, so you read `balances.length`, which differs from a String's `length()` method and a collection's `size()` method. The array size is fixed at creation and cannot change; to grow you allocate a new, larger array and copy, which is exactly what ArrayList does internally. Indices are zero-based and bounded, so accessing an index below zero or at or above length throws `ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException`.

Default element values are assigned automatically when the array is created with new, which is a key difference from local variables that must be explicitly initialized. For the integer types byte, short, int, and long the default is zero. For floating types float and double the default is zero point zero. For boolean it is false. For char it is the null character with code value zero. For every reference type, including String and any class, the default is null. So `new int[3]` is three zeros, `new boolean[2]` is two falses, and `new String[2]` is two nulls, which means iterating a freshly created object array and calling a method on an element without assigning it first throws a NullPointerException.

Multi-dimensional arrays are arrays of arrays, so `int[][] grid = new int[3][4]` makes three rows each of four zero-initialized ints, and a jagged array `int[][] j = new int[3][]` makes three null rows you size individually. The convention point is about where the brackets go. Both `int[] a` and `int a[]` are legal and mean the same thing, but the recommended style is `int[] a` because the brackets describe the type, so `int[]` reads as array-of-int. The post-variable form becomes confusing in multi-variable declarations, because `int[] a, b;` makes both a and b arrays, whereas `int a[], b;` makes a an array but b a plain int, which is a subtle, easy-to-miss bug. Putting the brackets on the type avoids that trap.

A senior engineer adds a few practical notes. Arrays are covariant, so a String array can be assigned to an Object array reference, but writing an incompatible element throws an `ArrayStoreException` at runtime, which is a known hole in array type safety that generics avoid. For bulk work you use `Arrays.fill` to set a default, `Arrays.copyOf` to resize, and `System.arraycopy` for fast copying. For money, an array of BigDecimal starts as all nulls, so you must populate it before use, and you never use a primitive double array for currency. And when a fixed-size, index-addressable, primitive-friendly structure is what you need, an array is the right tool, otherwise an ArrayList gives you dynamic growth.
sections.s3_banking:
National Bank of India tracks a fixed set of twelve monthly closing balances per account for a yearly statement, and a few array basics caused real confusion.

Problem 1 — a developer created an array of twelve BigDecimal monthly balances with new and then immediately tried to add them up without populating, hitting a NullPointerException, because a reference-type array defaults every slot to null. This is exactly the default-value rule for reference types.

Problem 2 — a declaration written as month count and balances on one line using the post-variable bracket style accidentally made only one of two variables an array, so a second counter that was meant to be a plain int was, and a sibling variable silently had the wrong type. This is exactly why the brackets belong on the type.

Problem 3 — the team needed both a blank twelve-slot array to fill month by month and a pre-seeded array of opening figures, illustrating the new form versus the initializer form, and they needed to read length rather than call size.

The fix populates the reference array before summing, uses the type-side bracket convention, and shows both creation forms along with default values for int, boolean, and reference arrays. The code defines an `Account`, a `MonthlyBalanceService` with a `blankYear` method returning a twelve-slot array, a `seedOpening` method using an initializer, and a `sum` method that safely handles nulls. The demo builds Rajesh's year, shows defaults, and sums.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: an int array of size three, a boolean array of size two, a String array of size two, a twelve-slot BigDecimal year array, and a three-element seeded opening array.

Step 1. The int array created with new has three slots, each automatically set to the int default of zero, so printing it shows three zeros. The boolean array shows two falses, and the String array shows two nulls. This demonstrates the default-value rule for primitive and reference types directly.

Step 2. The blankYear method returns a BigDecimal array of twelve slots. Because BigDecimal is a reference type, every slot defaults to null. The demo logs month zero, which is null, reproducing the NullPointerException hazard if you summed without populating.

Step 3. The demo populates each of the twelve months with a value derived from Rajesh's balance, so every slot now holds a BigDecimal. The populate loop reads year.length, the public final field, to bound the iteration.

Step 4. The sum method iterates the twelve months, skipping any that are still null as a defensive measure, and adds the rest into a BigDecimal total. Because all twelve are populated, the total is the full sum.

Step 5. The seedOpening method uses the initializer form, which both creates and fills the array in a single expression, returning a three-element array of opening balances. The demo reads its length as three and prints the first element.

Step 6. The demo logs the defaults, the null first month, the year total, and the seeded array details, and notes that length is a field read without parentheses, in contrast to a String length method or a collection size method.

Final output:

2026-10-30 18:55:40 [INFO] int[] defaults   = [0, 0, 0]
2026-10-30 18:55:40 [INFO] boolean[] default= [false, false]
2026-10-30 18:55:40 [INFO] String[] default = [null, null]
2026-10-30 18:55:40 [WARNING] fresh BigDecimal[] month 0 = null (null!)

sections.s5b_flow:
```
  ── Creation forms ──
  new int[5]            → [0,0,0,0,0]                 (defaults)
  int[] a = {1,2,3}     → [1,2,3]                     (initializer)
  new int[]{1,2,3}      → [1,2,3]                     (anonymous)

  ── Default element values when created with new ──
  byte/short/int/long → 0      float/double → 0.0
  boolean → false              char → '\u0000'
  reference (String, BigDecimal, ...) → null

  ── Monthly balance journey ──
  blankYear() → new BigDecimal[12] → [null x12]
       │ month 0 == null  (NPE risk if summed now)
       ▼ populate loop (i=0..length-1)
  [1000000.00, 1001000.00, ... 1011000.00]
       │ sum() skips nulls, adds the rest
       ▼
  total = 12066000.00

  length is a FIELD: year.length (no parentheses)
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
A Java array is a fixed-size, contiguous container of elements of a single type, and it is a heap object with a public final length field. I create one either with new, as in new int of size five, which allocates the slots already set to the type's default, or with an array initializer in braces, which both creates and fills the array and infers the size from the elements. There is also an anonymous array form using new with braces for passing directly or reassigning. The braces-only initializer is legal only at the point of declaration, so to assign later I use the new-with-braces form.

Default element values are assigned automatically when the array is created with new, which is different from local variables that must be explicitly initialized. The integer types default to zero, the floating types to zero point zero, boolean to false, char to the null character, and every reference type to null. That last one is the common trap: a freshly created array of objects such as String or BigDecimal has every slot null, so iterating and using an element before assigning it throws a NullPointerException.

On style, both int-brackets-a and int-a-brackets are legal and mean the same thing, but the convention is to put the brackets on the type, because the brackets are part of the type and int-brackets reads as array-of-int. The post-variable form becomes a real bug in a multi-variable declaration, because int-brackets a comma b makes both arrays, whereas int a-brackets comma b makes a an array but b a plain int. Putting the brackets on the type avoids that silent mismatch. I also remember that length is a field read without parentheses, unlike a String's length method or a collection's size method, and that the size is fixed at creation, so growing means allocating a new array and copying, which is what ArrayList does internally.

In our yearly statement builder at National Bank of India, a developer created a twelve-slot BigDecimal array of monthly balances with new and tried to sum them immediately, hitting a NullPointerException because every reference slot defaults to null, which I fixed by populating the months before summing and adding a null-safe accumulation. We also had a declaration written with the post-variable bracket style that accidentally made a sibling counter a plain int instead of an array, which is exactly why I enforce brackets-on-the-type in reviews. I use a fixed-size array here because the set of months is fixed and index-addressable, and I would reach for an ArrayList only when the size needs to grow dynamically.

---

keyPoints: Declaration: int[] arr or int arr[] — int[] preferred style
Initialization: new int[5] or {1, 2, 3} or new int[]{1, 2, 3}
Default values: 0 for int, null for objects, false for boolean
Fixed size — cannot grow after creation, use ArrayList for dynamic sizing
